visual_source_files.evidence: The PDF p.25 author link and repository README identify this repository as the original code for the paper. The notebook cell sets text.usetex=True, figsize=(9.5,2), RdBu, red/blue labels, orange/limegreen correctness, magenta payments, hidden ticks, and a three-panel schematic matching Figure 1.

Notebook cells for payment_m and payment_accuracy set the plasma six-series Figure 2 panels, inset, markers, grids, dimensions, and labels; the combined-panels cell sets GridSpec(2,4), viridis, loss/value markers, legends, and axes matching Figure 3.

The repository notebook cell creates Figure 5’s two panels with figsize=(14,5), four m series, explicit #1f77b4/#ff7f0e/#2ca02c/#d62728/#9467bd-style palette, circle markers, linewidth=2, dashed grid, and Gamma-shape category labels.
The linked repository script defines T=20, D=2 Gaussian settings, M_LIST from 20 to 201, K_LIST=[2,4,6,8], an SVM-exact baseline, and the single-panel payer-count overlay matching Figure 6.

The notebook computes exact/random/one-shot payment summaries and mean objective calls used by Table 2, but no independent LaTeX/table export or exact full-table styling source was found, so it is calculation support only.

source_acquisition.search_note: The inventory row in reports/tables/visual_source_inventory.csv is no_public_source_found with candidates socialfoundations/folktables and BML-Technion/accuracy_auctions; corpus/visual_sources/icml-2026-1d55d472edbc/ is empty. PDF p.25 explicitly links both repositories. Read-only gh metadata confirms the BML README says “original code for Welfare-Optimal Classification with Accuracy Auctions,” while folktables is a Census-derived data repository. The BML tree has the matched notebooks/script but no paper .tex/.tikz/.pgf/.svg or independent Table 1/3 generator. Exact-title GitHub code searches found no Figure 4 title match, so Figure 4 and Tables 1, D.3, and 3 remain without verified visual source; Table 2 has only partial calculation support.

paper_style.palette_strategy: Figures mix source-specific semantic colors (Figure 1), sequential plasma/viridis sweeps (Figures 2–3), and Matplotlib default categorical cycles (Figures 5–6); tables remain black-and-white. Series identity is frequently color-only, with marker redundancy used only in selected multi-group panels.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: Figures 1–3 and 5–6 are predominantly vector objects with embedded fonts. Figure 4 contains two JPEG raster image objects (1234×554 at about 403 ppi and 600×400 at about 196 ppi) inside otherwise vector PDF text/captions. Tables and pseudo-code are vector text/rules.
paper_style.style_consistency: Serif Nimbus Roman/Computer Modern dominates body/table text, while Matplotlib figures use DejaVu Sans and Figure 1 uses TeX/CMSS. The role split is understandable, but Figure 4’s JPEG typography and independent palette reduce consistency; caption completeness and uncertainty conventions also vary.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1. Accuracy auction induced by a classification algorithm. (Left) Each training point represents a participant in the auction: color represents label, and size represents value of accurate prediction. (Center) Welfare-maximizing allocation of pointwise accuracy via weighted loss minimization, showing learned score function (background color), decision boundary (dashed line), and prediction correctness (point color). (Right) User payments (size depicts magnitude) guarantee truthful elicitation, despite being highly sparse.

color.semantic_mapping: Left red/blue points encode binary labels; point area encodes value. Center orange/limegreen encodes correct/incorrect prediction; background diverging color encodes the learned score. Right magenta point area encodes positive payment magnitude; pale red/blue background is the decision-score field.

encodings.x: x1; schematic coordinate with hidden ticks, not a quantitative axis
encodings.y: x2; schematic coordinate with hidden ticks, not a quantitative axis
encodings.color: label in (a), prediction correctness in (b), and positive payment in (c); background is learned score
encodings.line: dashed learned decision boundary in the center and right panels
encodings.facet: three stages: training participants, accuracy allocation, and payments
encodings.text: panel headers plus accuracy/welfare and #payers/total pay annotations

figures.data_and_statistics: A synthetic two-dimensional mechanism illustration, not a population estimate. The left panel shows roughly 100 training points with bids/values; the center shows classifier correctness and a learned score; the right shows only positive payments. The source notebook uses a 100-point bid grid for the payment illustration, so the displayed accuracy, welfare, and total-payment annotations are illustrative rather than a precision estimate.
figures.evidence_relation: Connects the introduction claim that accuracy is an allocatable resource to the weighted loss objective and truthful-payment construction in Sections 3–6. It is the method interface from features/labels/bids to classifier-induced allocation and sparse payments, rather than an ablation or uncertainty result.
design_strengths: The fixed coordinate frame makes the input-to-allocation-to-payment transition legible.
Point area makes heterogeneous value and sparse payment burden visible while the dashed boundary anchors the classifier.
The caption explains the three principal visual encodings and states the truthful-elicitation implication.
design_weaknesses: Point area changes meaning from value to payment across adjacent panels and relies on the caption because there is no legend.
Hidden ticks prevent quantitative reading of the background, coordinates, and annotations.
The center panel layers score field, boundary, correctness, and points, creating crowding near the boundary; welfare and payment units are not defined.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a fixed three-stage canvas for mechanism interfaces: inputs, learned allocation, and economic outcome. If reused, add a compact legend or redundant shape/label encoding so value and payment area cannot be confused.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2. User payments under class-conditional multivariate Gaussian data. (Left) Number of paying users for increasing sample size and increasing variance (σ). (Right) Percentage of paying users as a function of model accuracy across varying class-mean distances and for increasing dimension (d).

color.semantic_mapping: Plasma sequence orders six σ series in the left panel and six d series in the right panel; inset orange is percent pay and blue is percent candidate. The series identity is otherwise carried by the legend.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: inside upper-left/top-left in each main panel; inset legend inside

encodings.x: train-set size m on the left; model accuracy on the right; both are continuous linear axes
encodings.y: number of paying users on the left; percentage of paying users on the right; inset reports percent pay/candidate
encodings.color: six σ values on the left and six class-mean-distance/d values on the right via plasma; orange/blue identify inset quantities
encodings.shape: circle markers on every sampled point
encodings.line: solid connecting lines for each parameter series
encodings.facet: two main panels plus a d=8 inset within the right panel
encodings.text: axis titles, legends, and a d=8 inset annotation; no direct series labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Synthetic class-conditional isotropic Gaussian experiments. The left fixes d=16, mean distance and v=1 while varying sample size m and σ; the right fixes m=500 and σ=1 while varying dimension and class-mean distance to control accuracy. Curves summarize repeated random trials, but no trial count, seed, error bar, or band is visible.
figures.evidence_relation: Turns the bounded-payer claim in Theorem 2 into a sample-size/variance plateau and relates accuracy to the percentage paying. The inset exposes candidate versus payer sets and links the main curves to the candidate-set argument in Lemma 2.
design_strengths: Both panels preserve the same payer outcome, making the two controlled questions easy to compare.
The inset distinguishes candidate points from actual payers rather than hiding the intermediate algorithmic set.
Parameter sweeps are directly shown with markers and a monotone sequential palette.
design_weaknesses: Six series in a narrow single-column figure are distinguished almost entirely by color, which is weak in grayscale and for color-vision deficiencies.
No uncertainty or repeat count is shown, so small curve differences can look more definitive than the evidence supports.
The caption omits λ, m, mean-distance settings, and the trial/aggregation definition; inset and main percentage scales are not explicitly reconciled.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair a scale-law panel with a controlled accuracy/cost panel and use an inset for the algorithmic intermediate set. Preserve the pattern but add line/marker redundancy and trial/uncertainty metadata.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3. Welfare, accuracy, and payments on the folktables dataset. (Left) Tradeoff in accuracy vs. welfare under feature-based values for increasing valuation dispersion (controlled by v+). (Center-left) Tradeoff in accuracy vs. welfare under label-based values for increasing valuation gap (controlled by v+). (Center-right) For label-based values, per-class and overall welfare (top) and accuracy (bottom) when optimizing welfare (α = 1). (Right) For label-based values, number (top) and percentage (bottom) of paying users under different losses complying with Thm. 2 for increasing sample size m.

color.semantic_mapping: Viridis samples encode valuation settings in the first two Pareto panels; default blue/orange/green plus black encode loss or value-group variants in the paired panels. Marker shape distinguishes +1/−1/Both and hinge/squared-hinge/log-loss variants.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: inside upper-left in Pareto panels; upper panel legends shared by vertical pairs

encodings.x: accuracy or welfare in the two Pareto panels; valuation ratio/gap in center-right; sample size m in right; continuous linear axes
encodings.y: normalized welfare/accuracy in Pareto panels, welfare and accuracy in center-right, and payer count/percent in right
encodings.color: viridis valuation settings in the first two panels; default categorical colors and black for losses/value groups in later panels
encodings.shape: circles in Pareto panels; circles/squares/triangles for +1/−1/Both and hinge/squared-hinge/log-loss
encodings.line: solid connecting lines; Pareto traces and within-group sweeps
encodings.facet: GridSpec(2,4): two full-height Pareto panels, two vertical welfare/accuracy panels, and two vertical payer-count/percent panels
encodings.text: six panel titles, axis labels, legends, and α=1 annotation in the center-right pair

figures.data_and_statistics: Folktables ACSIncome/NJ semi-synthetic values. The first two panels trace weighted SVM/logistic tradeoffs over α; the center-right changes label-value gaps; the right compares three losses over m=1000–4000 with λ=10^3/√m. Curves are random-split/generation summaries with no visible seed, trial count, or uncertainty; normalized welfare scales differ across Pareto panels.
figures.evidence_relation: Serves as the main empirical bridge from the welfare objective to accuracy tradeoffs, group allocation, and Theorem 2 payer scaling. Its left/center panels instantiate welfare-versus-accuracy mechanisms, while the right panels recover loss-dependent cost patterns; Appendix C/D provide settings and sensitivity expansions.
design_strengths: The page-width composition closes a narrative loop from global Pareto tradeoff to group allocation and payment cost.
Vertically paired panels reuse the x axis and marker shapes to expose both total and proportional outcomes.
The object connects the paper’s strongest theoretical and empirical claims in one visual evidence chain.
design_weaknesses: Six axes and many curves are compressed into a very shallow canvas; tick labels and legends are hard to read at page scale.
The first two normalized welfare axes are not directly comparable, but the shared visual treatment can suggest that they are.
Fine Pareto differences lack uncertainty, and the caption omits α interpolation, denominator, seed/repetition, and λ schedule details.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a page-width multi-panel bridge that moves from overall tradeoff to subgroup mechanism and finally to deployment cost. For a high-density version, move definitions and uncertainty to a companion table or interactive view.

figures.label: Figure 4

color.semantic_mapping: Raster panel (a) uses orange/green interval labels and grey guides; panel (b) uses blue Welfare, green Accuracy, red 0–1 Loss, and grey dashed threshold references. Values are estimated from rendered JPEG pixels.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: upper-left in panel (b); none in panel (a)

encodings.x: sampled one-dimensional x coordinate in panel (a); threshold θ in panel (b), both displayed linearly
encodings.y: directly labeled class intervals in panel (a); Metric Value in panel (b)
encodings.color: orange/green class labels in the construction; blue Welfare, green Accuracy, red 0–1 Loss in the scan
encodings.line: solid metric curves plus grey dashed threshold/reference lines at approximately θ=0.5 and θ=1
encodings.facet: (a) sampled data construction and (b) accuracy/average-welfare/loss versus threshold
encodings.text: direct y=1/y=0 labels, panel titles, metric legend, and θ reference cues

figures.data_and_statistics: Constructive Appendix D.1 example: x is uniformly sampled on [0,1.5], with y=0 on [0,0.5], y~Ber(0.5) on [0.5,1], and y=1 on [1,1.5]; v0=1 and v1=3. The right panel scans θ and reports accuracy, welfare, and 0–1 loss. It is an analytical counterexample-style construction, not a repeated estimate, and has no uncertainty display.
figures.evidence_relation: Makes visible the claim that the accuracy optimum can be non-unique while welfare differs across thresholds, motivating the value-aware objective. It supports the theory mechanism but is not tied to the payment-cost tables.
design_strengths: The data-generating interval picture and objective scan sit side by side, allowing the threshold behavior to be traced back to the construction.
Dashed reference lines separate the accuracy plateau endpoint from the welfare-optimal threshold.
The compact two-panel form is appropriate for a theorem counterexample.
design_weaknesses: The two embedded JPEGs are visibly softer than the paper’s vector plots, especially for small labels and curve edges.
Panel (a) has no probability/vertical scale and the caption does not state intervals, values, or the key conclusion.
Colors differ from the rest of the paper and do not robustly survive grayscale; panel (b) requires Appendix prose to interpret θ=1.
figures.reusable_pattern: Place a construction diagram beside a parameter/objective scan to explain a counterexample. Put the interval rules, value weights, and highlighted optimum in the caption or direct labels, and export both panels as vector when possible.

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5. Payments and % Payers under varying valuation variance and dataset sizes m.

color.semantic_mapping: Matplotlib default cycle maps the four m values (2000, 5000, 10000, 20000) consistently across Average Payment and % Payers panels.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: inside plot area; legend title m

encodings.x: categorical Gamma shape parameter k: const, 16, 4, 1, 0.5, and approximately 0.33
encodings.y: Average Payment in the left panel and % Payers in the right, both linear
encodings.color: dataset size m, with four explicit default-cycle colors shared across panels
encodings.line: solid lines connect the categorical means; source sets linewidth=2
encodings.facet: two parallel response panels with the same category order
encodings.text: titles, Gamma shape parameter k x-label, metric y-labels, and m legend

figures.data_and_statistics: Gaussian class-conditional simulation with d=8, fixed mean separation and mean value 1. Constant values and Gamma values with k∈{16,4,1,0.5,0.33} hold the mean while changing variance; m∈{2000,5000,10000,20000}. Panels report average payment and payer percentage, with no error bars, bands, or replicate counts.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix D.5 sensitivity check for the mechanism statement that valuation heterogeneity modestly affects average payment while payer proportion is comparatively stable. It complements Figure 3’s value dispersion and Figure 2’s payer scaling.
design_strengths: The two response metrics share the same variance axis and allow level-versus-incidence comparison.
The explicit m palette remains consistent across both panels.
Source linewidth=2 preserves legibility after page-width reduction.
design_weaknesses: Connecting categories with lines implies a continuous/equidistant Gamma-shape scale even though the x axis is categorical.
Small right-panel differences have no uncertainty display, and four series rely on color alone in grayscale.
The caption omits Gamma/value definitions, m values, and replicate/aggregation details.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use parallel response panels with a shared categorical stressor and stable series colors to separate payment level from payer incidence. Add marker/line redundancy and uncertainty when the effect is small.

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6. Comparing number of payers in SVM vs. k-NN (Appendix D.6).

color.semantic_mapping: Default Matplotlib cycle identifies k-NN k=2/4/6/8 and SVM-exact; the legend supplies the model identity.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: inside right side of the panel

encodings.x: sample size per class m, 19 roughly linear values from 20 to 201
encodings.y: number of paying users, linear and clipped/displayed from 0 to 100
encodings.color: five model families: KNN k=2/4/6/8 and SVM-exact
encodings.shape: circle markers at sampled m values
encodings.text: title, axis labels, and in-panel model legend; no direct labels

figures.data_and_statistics: exp_knn.py uses T=20 trials, D=2, μ=(0.25,0), σ=1, m=20–201 per class, K_LIST={2,4,6,8}, and a SVM-exact baseline. The y outcome is positive critical-payment payer count. No error bars or replicate spread are shown; large-k curves reach the y=100 display ceiling.
figures.evidence_relation: Places Theorem 3’s k-NN Ω(m) behavior next to Theorem 2’s bounded-payer SVM behavior on a common finite Gaussian setting. It is the cleanest theory-to-model-family overlay in the appendix, with D.6 supplying the construction details.
design_strengths: One y axis and one sample-size axis make the slope/platform contrast immediately visible.
The in-panel legend identifies k variants without consuming another panel.
The source parameters are deterministic and directly tied to the appendix experiment.
design_weaknesses: The finite d=2 Gaussian setup and 20 trials do not establish behavior for all distributions or k-NN settings.
The y=100 limit clips/presses the largest curves, hiding their continuation.
Five lines rely mainly on color and have no uncertainty; the caption omits d, σ, T, k ranges, and clipping.
figures.reusable_pattern: Overlay model families with a shared outcome and unit to visualize contrasting theoretical growth rates. State the finite-sample setting, repetitions, and plotting ceiling in the caption.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1. Comparison of payment algorithms. O is the learning objective, \tilde m the number of candidate points, k the number of search steps, N the number of (possible) random draws. Typically N ≪ k, and we expect \tilde m ≪ m. For SVM in particular, \tilde m is constant, and calls to O require only a subset of data points.

tables.uncertainty: None. DSIC, IR, and critical-bid cells are symbolic properties (✓, E, ×), not intervals or empirical uncertainty.
tables.data_and_statistics: Theoretical comparison of stable search/random/one-shot variants and a non-stable alternative. Columns are algorithm, calls to O, DSIC, IR, and p_i=b_i^c. Call formulas are symbolic and the table contains no empirical runtime, repeated trials, or decimal estimates.
tables.evidence_relation: Condenses the stability screening and Algorithm 1 into a guarantee-versus-objective-call decision surface. It connects the method’s payment algorithms to the later Appendix D.2 empirical calls/welfare table.
design_strengths: Calls, incentive properties, individual rationality, and critical-bid behavior appear in one compact decision surface.
Stable/non-stable row grouping exposes the applicability boundary quickly.
The caption defines the symbols needed to interpret the formulas without requiring a separate legend.
design_weaknesses: The E symbol is not expanded in a table-side key, and tilde-m symbols are compressed in a narrow column.
No measured runtime or variance is provided, so readers must align symbolic calls with Table 2 themselves.
The caption defines symbols but does not explicitly state which rows are approximate/expected guarantees.
tables.reusable_pattern: For algorithm variants whose value lies in a guarantee–cost tradeoff, combine grouped rows with property columns and symbolic call complexity, and define every symbol in the caption.

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2. Payment algorithms – comparison between exact and randomized

tables.uncertainty: Total payments include mean, stdev, min, and max; calls to O and welfare are means. The caption does not define trial count or the aggregation level, and negative one-shot means indicate rebates/negative payments in the visible values.
tables.data_and_statistics: Nine rows cover exact, random N=1/3/6/9, and one-shot μ=0.25/0.4/0.5/0.6/0.75. A grouped total-payments (m=1000) header spans mean/stdev/min/max, followed by mean calls to O and mean welfare. Decimal precision is mixed: payment means show more digits than other columns. The public notebook supports the calculation logic but not a complete LaTeX/table export.
tables.evidence_relation: Empirically compares Algorithms 2–4: exact is the payment baseline, random N trades objective calls for variance, and one-shot trades one call for higher variance/bias. It operationalizes the efficiency discussion after Table 1.
design_strengths: Payment, objective-call cost, and welfare share one table, putting deployment tradeoffs on the same decision surface.
The increasing random-N rows make the intended variance/cost progression visible.
The grouped header separates distributional payment summaries from mean cost and welfare.
design_weaknesses: The caption is too short to define m=1000, column statistics, repetitions, or one-shot μ.
Mean/stdev/min/max values are visually crowded and the visible ordering is not intuitive for the exact row; the table needs an explicit statistic-level note.
No highlighter, runtime unit, or repeated-trial count helps readers identify the preferred operating point.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a grouped “cost + welfare + distribution summary” table for mechanism variants, but define the replicate level, denominator, negative payment/rebate semantics, and every statistic in the caption.

tables.label: Appendix D.3 calls table

caption.text: D.3. Payment Algorithms – Theoretical Comparison Between Exact and Randomized. Payment algorithm / # calls to O.

tables.uncertainty: None. This is a symbolic objective-call count: exact 1+r+z·k, random 1+r+z·n, and one-shot 1; it does not express runtime variance or welfare uncertainty.
tables.data_and_statistics: Three payment algorithms are compared in two columns. The surrounding D.3 prose defines m, r, z, k, and n; the table itself contains only formulas and no measured values.
tables.evidence_relation: Provides the smallest symbolic bridge between Table 1’s candidate/search notation, Algorithms 2–4, and Appendix D.2’s measured mean calls. It is a reproduction/complexity aid rather than a performance result.
design_strengths: Minimal formula presentation makes the relative objective-call counts immediately readable.
Each formula corresponds directly to an algorithm and the prose variables.
No decorative grid or redundant columns compete with the central comparison.
design_weaknesses: The object has no independent number/caption in the PDF; without the preceding prose, m/r/z/k/n are undefined.
The one-shot value 1 counts only objective calls and does not signal its welfare bias or variance.
A reader can mistake symbolic calls for wall-clock runtime without an explicit unit/boundary note.
tables.reusable_pattern: Keep a compact formula table for complexity, but give it a number and self-contained variable definitions so symbolic calls cannot be mistaken for measured runtime.

tables.label: Table 3

caption.text: Table 3. Varying loss and λ-regularization parameter with increasing m- dataset sizes.

tables.uncertainty: None. Values are configuration summaries for payer count, payer percentage, and test accuracy; no interval, spread, rank, or replicate count is displayed.
tables.data_and_statistics: Twenty-four rows group hinge, log, and squared-hinge losses across eight c(m)/λ schedules. Four m columns appear under each of Number of Payers, Percent Pay, and Test Accuracy, for m=1000/2000/4000/10000. Most values have three decimals; c(m) uses mixed m, m/10^q, and √m schedules. C/c(m) and λ=1/C notation are mixed between table and prose.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix D.4 tests whether the Figure 3 right-side payer pattern persists across losses and regularization schedules while retaining accuracy. It links the Theorem 2 conditions to sensitivity evidence rather than introducing a new mechanism.
design_strengths: Payer count, payer percentage, and test accuracy are aligned on one decision surface.
Loss row groups and schedule rows make the sensitivity grid complete enough to locate high-payer versus low-payer regimes.
Grouped metric headers repeat the same m values, supporting within-m comparisons.
design_weaknesses: The 24×14 layout is dense at page scale; roots, exponents, and schedule labels are easy to misread.
No uncertainty, repetitions, or significance marking distinguishes robust effects from configuration noise.
Changing c(m)/λ along with m means rows are not a direct fixed-λ test, while the caption does not clarify that boundary.
tables.reusable_pattern: For parameter sensitivity, align cost, incidence, and quality metrics under repeated m columns and group by loss. Freeze C/λ notation and replicate definitions in the table header or caption.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 establishes the bids→weighted classifier allocation→sparse payment interface; Table 1 formalizes guarantee/call tradeoffs; Figures 2–3 move from synthetic payer scaling to folktables welfare/accuracy/payment evidence; Appendix Figure 4, Table 2, the D.3 calls table, Table 3, Figure 5, and Figure 6 add the constructive gap, payment variance/cost, symbolic complexity, loss/λ sensitivity, value-variance, and SVM–k-NN contrasts.
cross_object_system.caption_system: Captions use italic Figure/Table labels, short titles, and panel/setup/comparison prose. Figure 1 comes closest to stating a finding; most others leave findings to the body. Trial count, seed, uncertainty, normalization, and denominator definitions are generally absent, and the unnumbered D.3 table has no standalone caption.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: The theoretical table uses property columns, while empirical tables use grouped metric headers with repeated m columns and row groups. Table 2’s payment distribution group and Table 3’s metric groups share the same top-level-first structure, but statistic-level and C/λ definitions are not consistently self-contained.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Figure 1 and Table 1 are method/theory interfaces; Figures 2–3 are main results; Table 2/D.3 and Figures 4–6 extend costs, counterexamples, sensitivity, and model-family comparison. The paper’s prose calls the objects in this order, so the method→result→appendix evidence chain is present but distributed across pages.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Main text retains the mechanism, Theorem 2/3 claims, and Figures 1–3; Appendices A–B give proofs/algorithms, C gives data/model details, and D provides Tables 2–3 plus Figures 4–6. Figure 6 points to D.6 explicitly, while Figure 3 does not name the specific C/D subsections needed for replication.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Body/table Nimbus Roman and Computer Modern are stable at roughly 10 pt; figure text is sans-serif at roughly 6.5–12 pt, with TeX math. Figure 4’s raster-internal typography is the largest mismatch and the dense Figure 3/Table 3 text is difficult at page scale.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: There is no global semantic palette: Figure 1 uses red/blue/orange/limegreen/magenta, Figure 2 plasma, Figure 3 viridis plus defaults, Figures 5–6 defaults, and tables black-and-white. Color often carries the only series identity, limiting cross-figure reuse and grayscale accessibility.

most_reusable_patterns: Figure 1’s fixed three-stage mechanism chain from input to allocation to payment.
Figure 3’s page-width sequence from overall Pareto tradeoff through group allocation to payer cost.
Table 1’s grouped guarantee/property and objective-call decision surface.
highest_value_objects: Figure 1, because it makes the auction mechanism and sparse truthful payment interface visible.
Figure 3, because it connects welfare, accuracy, allocation, and payments on folktables in one evidence bridge.
Figure 6, because it overlays the bounded SVM and growing k-NN payer behaviors on common axes.
Table 2, because it places payment, calls, welfare, and payment spread together, although its statistic labels need clarification.
failure_patterns: Narrow plots with many color-only series and little grayscale/line-style redundancy.
Captions that omit trials, uncertainty, normalization, denominators, or key controlled settings.
Table 2’s visually unintuitive statistic columns and Table 3’s high-density loss×schedule grid.
Figure 4’s unmatched JPEG source and mixed raster typography.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: Build a mechanism interface around value–accuracy–payment, then use a dense main comparison and appendix cost/sensitivity/model overlays to map theory to finite experiments, relying on body text to resolve palette semantics, statistic levels, and applicability boundaries.
